topicName: Full Refresh vs Append vs Upsert (Merge) Operations
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Technical Tutorial: Full Refresh vs Append vs Upsert Operations in ETL"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Designing an Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) pipeline requires choosing the right data loading strategy. The choice directly impacts pipeline performance, resource consumption, storage costs, and data accuracy. This tutorial explores the three primary loading strategies: Full Refresh, Append, and Upsert (Merge)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Full Refresh Strategy"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Full Refresh strategy truncates or drops the target table and reloads it completely from the source during every pipeline run. It guarantees that the target is an exact mirror of the source, eliminating issues with stale data, duplicates, or missing deletions."},{"order":5,"bullet_point":"Pros: Simple to implement, guarantees absolute data consistency, handles source deletions seamlessly."},{"order":6,"bullet_point":"Cons: High network and compute overhead, poor scalability for large datasets, downtime or unavailability during the reload window."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"TRUNCATE TABLE target_table;
INSERT INTO target_table (id, name, updated_at)
SELECT id, name, updated_at FROM source_table;"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Append Strategy"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"The Append strategy inserts newly arrived source data directly into the target table without modifying or checking existing records. It is the fastest loading method and is ideal for immutable data streams such as audit logs, IoT sensor telemetry, and clickstream events."},{"order":10,"bullet_point":"Pros: Extremely fast execution, minimal resource consumption, preserves historical state."},{"order":11,"bullet_point":"Cons: Does not handle updates to existing records, risks creating duplicate entries if not managed, does not capture deletions."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"INSERT INTO target_table (event_id, event_data, timestamp)
SELECT event_id, event_data, timestamp
FROM source_table
WHERE timestamp > (SELECT MAX(timestamp) FROM target_table);"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Upsert (Merge) Strategy"},{"order":14,"paragraph":"The Upsert (Update + Insert), or Merge, strategy checks if a record already exists in the target table based on a unique business key. If it exists, the record is updated with new values. If it does not exist, a new record is inserted. This strategy is essential for mutable dimensions like user profiles or product catalogs."},{"order":15,"bullet_point":"Pros: Keeps data current, avoids duplicates, highly efficient compared to full refreshes for large tables."},{"order":16,"bullet_point":"Cons: Complex SQL syntax, higher compute costs due to join and match operations, requires well-defined primary keys."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"MERGE INTO target_table AS t
USING source_table AS s
ON t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET t.name = s.name, t.updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (id, name, updated_at) VALUES (s.id, s.name, s.updated_at);"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary and Best Practices"},{"order":19,"bullet_point":"Use Full Refresh for small lookup tables (< 100k rows) or when data lineage is complex and rebuilding is safer."},{"order":20,"bullet_point":"Use Append for append-only transaction logs, metrics, and event streaming pipelines."},{"order":21,"bullet_point":"Use Upsert for large dimension tables and operational databases where entity states change frequently."}]
